title: Attachment to things
hook: phones and possessions that own us
tomorrow: Bebe says she's going home soon. does Simran let her go?

segments.voice: Yesterday, greed in the shop: lobh wants the next thing, and santokh says enough. Now, a glow under a blanket.

Two in the morning. Simran is on the couch, since Bebe has her room, and her phone is still in her hand. She meant to check one thing. That was an hour ago. Her thumb keeps moving on its own, and when she sets the phone down on the floor, her hand drifts back to it. A video ends and the next one starts by itself. She isn't even enjoying it anymore. Across the hall, Bebe's lamp clicks on, and a sleepy voice says: putt, who's holding whom?
screen: `2 A.M., ONE MORE SCROLL.` → `THE HAND DRIFTS BACK.` → `BEBE: WHO'S HOLDING WHOM?`

segments.voice: The Sikh word is moh: attachment, one of the five thieves on ang 600. On ang 1358, Guru Arjan speaks to it, in paraphrase, as an unconquered warrior that overpowers even the mighty. That's not about a phone; it's anything we grip so tightly it starts gripping back. Today's line is free hands. Free hands doesn't mean empty hands. Bebe owns a garden, a closet of suits and a radio she loves. It means hands that can still put a thing down. Here's the test worth repeating: if you can't set it down for an hour, it's holding you. And that's been this whole week, in a way. Every family, one row at langar. A full place, for Bhua Kiran. Seva at home, when Bebe moved in. Breathe first, on the road. Softly at home, after the shout. Enough, at the checkout. Each one was a small letting go: of who belongs, of being the one in charge, of the last word, of one more thing. None of them asked for empty hands. Bebe kept her chilies; Simran kept her phone. They just loosened the grip. Simran slides the phone face down under the couch, out of reach. Her hand twitches toward it once, then settles. From the next room she can hear Bebe's slow breathing, the fridge humming, a car passing outside. Then she lies still and listens to the house breathe.
screen: `MOH: THE GRIP THAT GRIPS BACK.` · `FREE HANDS, NOT EMPTY HANDS.` · `A WEEK OF SMALL LETTING GO.` · then, large: `FREE HANDS.`

segments.voice: If your phone is near, turn it face down and slide it a little out of reach. Rest your hands open on your lap, palms up, empty for a while. Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and stay with that free feeling as you breathe.
Attachment to things. Moh, the thief that grips us back, and hands that can still put a thing down.
Free hands: hold things lightly enough to set them down. That's the week, gathered up.

howItsDone: Sikhs count attachment (moh) among the five thieves; the Gurus lived as householders with families and possessions, and the teaching is to live among things without being ruled by them.
